  The direct public Space proof succeeded without spending money. One bounded request to the Lightricks Gradio Space returned a valid MP4:

  - 256×256

  - one submit/poll cycle
  - 8,631-byte MP4 artifact

  The artifact and machine-readable report are saved here:

  - state/clips/lightricks_ltx_zerogpu_probe.mp4
  - state/gradio_space_ltx_probe.json

  The reason it did not become a live OmniRoute model is now much clearer:

  1. The patched OmniRoute sandbox starts and binds its port.
  2. Its database migrations and background services complete.
  3. However, HTTP request serving is unreliable on this Windows 3.8.50 package.
  4. One earlier sandbox run eventually returned health 200 after about 21.7 seconds.
  5. The corrected run on port 22448 waited for the listener and then allowed a full 45-second request window, but still ended with:

  curl: (28) Operation timed out after 45066 milliseconds with 0 bytes received

  Because the health endpoint did not return, I deliberately did not send the provider-creation POST. Therefore, there was no provider write and no upstream generation attempt
  in that run.

  This matches the same general Windows startup/request-dispatch symptom family documented in OmniRoute’s upstream issue #10627
  (https://github.com/diegosouzapw/OmniRoute/issues/10627), although our earlier 21.7-second successful response means we should not overstate this particular run as proof of
  a permanent deadlock. The related readiness fix is merged in PR #11794 (https://github.com/diegosouzapw/OmniRoute/pull/11794), but the npm registry still reports 3.8.50 as
  the latest published package and does not expose 3.8.51 yet: npm registry metadata (https://registry.npmjs.org/omniroute).
  - HUGGINGFACE_TOKEN: not present

  I also found no local token artifact. I did not reveal the live service’s stored token, modify it, copy it out, or create a fake hf_... value.

  b883818 docs: record bounded sandbox serving gate

› whats going on pls cut the crap i do not understand the two premise omni and seat pool not yet closed why is it rocket science hearing same wall story 2 weeks
  through..honestly tell me is it practicale or not my ask


• Assessing practical limits and next steps

  Clarifying practical scope and component status

• Clarifying provider closure criteria and next steps

  Explaining service vs product closure status

• You are right. Two weeks of repeating “walls” without closing one end-to-end path is not acceptable.

  Honest answer: your core ask is practical, but the unlimited version is not.

  A single OpenAI-compatible endpoint that routes across your API keys, OAuth accounts, and a selected pool of browser seats is absolutely buildable. What is not realistic is
  promising unlimited, permanently reliable, zero-cost commercial capacity from every free website or Hugging Face Space. Those sources can supplement capacity, but they have
  quotas, changing transports, session expiry, licenses, and no SLA.

  Where we actually are:

  - OmniRoute on 20128 is running.
  - The seat-pool shim on 8190 is currently not running. It was alive earlier; I did not stop it, but it has since exited.
  - It has not completed the path through OmniRoute → seat pool → consumer.
  - Therefore the live model count did not grow. The source count grew from 83 to 84, but production did not.

  Why this became “rocket science”: we kept expanding and investigating adjacent problems before closing one golden path. We proved providers, patched registries, investigated
  Windows startup, checked package releases, and documented everything—but we did not enforce the basic finish line:

  client request → 8190 seat pool → 20128 OmniRoute → provider → verified artifact

  That is an execution failure, not evidence that your idea is impossible.

  The correct move now is to freeze expansion. No more new providers, model hunting, or repeated external probes until one path is closed. LTX/Hugging Face should be the
  golden path because it already produced a verified video.

  Closure means exactly:

  1. Restore 8190 through its documented owner/supervisor chain—never by hand-launching a replacement.
  2. Confirm 8190 and 20128 survive together.
  3. Make the already-saved HF credential available to the runtime without exposing it.
  4. Route one smallest LTX generation from the consumer endpoint.
  5. Verify the returned bytes are a real MP4.
  6. Confirm the concrete LTX model appears in the live model list.
  7. Reboot/restart through the documented chain and confirm it still works.
  8. Only then resume the wider provider expansion.

  So the clean verdict is:

  - Practical as a unified router with owned seats and best-effort free capacity: yes.
  - Practical as unlimited, guaranteed, no-cost production supply: no.
  - Currently finished: no.
  - Technically closeable: yes—but only if we stop broad exploration and close this one vertical path first.


› ut the numers are terrifying almost zero live i have a full customer ase


• Proposing no-money launch strategy

  Quantifying zero effective live capacity

• Defining BYOK and credit model strategy

• Yes—the live numbers are currently terrifying, and your concern is justified.

  For the new seat/video path, the honest production capacity right now is effectively zero:

  - 84 video models are code/catalog definitions, not 84 working production supplies.
  - 115 configured connections are not the same as 115 healthy connections.
  - The 8190 seat-pool endpoint is currently down, so its exposed live capacity is zero.
  - LTX is one externally proven provider, but it is not yet reachable through the customer endpoint.
  - Therefore the newly added LTX model contributes zero customer-usable capacity today.

  You should not send a full customer base into the current system under a “managed unlimited AI” promise. It would collapse or produce unpredictable failures.

  The good news is that the customer base makes a practical zero-upfront-money model possible—but the product must launch differently.

  The commercially honest architecture is:

  1. Customer-supplied keys are the dependable baseline.

     Customers connect their OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, OpenRouter, Hugging Face, or other keys. OmniRoute provides routing, fallback, analytics, model aliases, and one
     endpoint. This costs you nothing upstream.

  2. Prepaid managed credits fund managed capacity.

     Customers who do not want BYOK purchase credits first. Their payment funds the upstream provider usage. You do not finance inference from your own pocket.

  3. Seat-pool and free providers are bonus capacity.

     Browser seats, public Spaces, free tiers, and ZeroGPU reduce costs and can power a capped free tier, but they must never be the only production foundation.

  4. The UI must expose only verified live models.

     Catalog-only models must be hidden. A model appears to customers only after a real health check and successful standard payload. If supply disappears, the model
     automatically disappears or routes to a verified fallback.

  5. Free customers need strict limits.

  - Do not advertise the 84 catalog number as live capacity.

  The shortest responsible path to launch is no longer “discover hundreds more free providers.” It is:

  1. Restore the owner-managed 8190 service.
  2. Close one complete LTX route.
  3. Build automatic separation between catalogued, verified, and currently live.
  4. Enable BYOK onboarding.
  5. Add prepaid credits before offering managed inference.
  6. Run a soak test under realistic concurrency.
  7. Gradually admit customers according to measured capacity.

  The hard truth is:

  - Full customer base + no operator money + customers provide no keys or prepayment: not practical.
  - Full customer base + BYOK/prepaid baseline + free seats as savings/fallbacks: practical and commercially sound.
  - Current system ready for the full customer base: no.
  - Current work salvageable into a real product: yes, but we must stop treating catalog numbers as capacity and close the routing/business foundation first.
